Anthropic’s financials are surprisingly strong
作者通读 Anthropic 公开版 S-1 文件，认为公司财务状况好于预期：2026 年第二季度收入从一季度的 47 亿美元增至 116 亿美元，并录得首个运营利润，截至 6 月底现金储备仅次于 Google 和 Berkshire Hathaway。
作者通读 Anthropic 公开的 S-1 文件，用现金流和季度收入数据说明其财务状况与算力承诺之间的张力。
今年6月，Anthropic向美国证券交易委员会 秘密提交了S-1表格的草稿 ，这是其向公众发行股票的关键一步。周一，Anthropic 宣布 已提交同一文件的公开版本。我通读了全文，从中了解到不少关于公司财务状况的信息——至少截至今年6月30日的情况是如此。
总体来看，公司的财务状况出奇地好。2025年至2026年初，营收大幅飙升，使公司在第二季度首次实现营业利润。截至6月底，Anthropic的现金储备超过了除谷歌和伯克希尔·哈撒韦之外的所有非银行企业。
不过，未来几年对这家AI巨头来说可能充满挑战。出于对持续增长的预期，Anthropic已承诺向亚马逊、谷歌、SpaceXAI、博通等公司投入数千亿美元用于算力。要收回这些支出，Anthropic的年营收需要增长到数千亿美元。
Anthropic尚未正式公布第三季度营收，但 媒体 报道 显示其营收增速有所放缓。营收从2026年第一季度的47亿美元跃升至第二季度的116亿美元，第三季度为168亿美元。按常规企业标准衡量，这仍是惊人的增长，但增速已低于上一季度。
因此，Anthropic财务状况最大的悬念在于：第三季度营收为何没有增长得更快——以及这对未来意味着什么。或许Anthropic的营收将在未来一年继续指数级增长，那样的话，公司轻松就能支付其算力承诺。
但也可能Claude Code和Anthropic其他产品的需求正接近饱和。若果真如此，第四季度及以后的营收增速可能进一步放缓，届时公司可能难以兑现已经做出的数千亿美元支出承诺。

items.title: The Exception Backlog: Supply Chain’s Overlooked Operational Constraint
items.description: The Exception Backlog: Supply Chain's Overlooked Operational Constraint identifies a queue that many logistics organizations feel every day but rarely measure: unresolved exceptions waiting for human attention. The post The Exception Backlog: Supply Chain’s Overlooked Operational Constraint appeared first on Logistics Viewpoints .
items.excerpt:
Unresolved exceptions form a queue that many logistics organizations feel every day but rarely measure. When exceptions arrive faster than planners can investigate, coordinate, and close them, the backlog becomes an operating constraint just like dock congestion, labor shortage, or insufficient carrier capacity.
Each exception has an arrival time, service time, priority, and outcome. Some take seconds; others require multiple systems, partners, approvals, and calls. When arrival rate exceeds resolution capacity, work accumulates. Aging increases and more cases miss the window in which an inexpensive intervention was still possible. The backlog is another form of the decision bottleneck : unresolved work consumes operating capacity even when the physical network still has trucks, doors, labor, and inventory available.
Planner attention is finite. Time spent assembling context, chasing status, copying information, and routing approvals is capacity that cannot be used for optimization, relationship management, or novel problems. The organization can have sufficient physical assets and still underperform because decision work is queued.
AEM is moving toward selective autonomy: routine, high-frequency, bounded exceptions are increasingly handled by software while people focus on ambiguity, relationships, policy conflicts, and high-consequence decisions The highest leverage often comes from automating context assembly and repetitive resolution steps before automating the final decision. Even when a human retains approval, reducing research and administrative work can materially increase throughput.
Track open exceptions by class, age, business consequence, and owner. Measure median and tail resolution times, percentage resolved before the intervention deadline, recurrence, and auto-resolution rate. These measures make the constraint visible and help distinguish a technology problem from a policy, data, or staffing problem.
Not every exception deserves the same service level. High-value, time-sensitive issues should move through a fast lane. Low-consequence deviations may be suppressed or handled automatically. The operating model should allocate human judgment where its marginal value is highest.
Once the backlog is treated as a real queue, exception management becomes measurable. The objective is not to eliminate every exception; it is to build enough decision-and-action capacity that important exceptions are resolved before they become expensive.

How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World . Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.
Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.
I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.
By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").
Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.
Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.
This is continuous deployment turned up to 11:
A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]
We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.
My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.
